title: Trajectories of legal work in the context of machine learning AI: conceptualising mediated evolution

author: James Faulconbridge

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Faulconbridge accepts the cluster’s core account of task-level reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement and materially extends it through a mediated-evolution framework: professional autonomy, partnership governance, identity and organisational context shape how automation and augmentation unfold. He also reinforces the cluster’s competence concern by identifying risks to junior learning, while treating them as reported concerns rather than established deskilling.
qs: Questions should focus less on “how many jobs” or the “life or death of the lawyer” and more on the way the tasks and role of a lawyer will evolve, in particular as some aspects of what a lawyer does is deemphasised because of the capabilities of ML, whilst other aspects are emphasised as automation and augmentation work hand-in-hand alongside lawyers to deliver the best possible services to clients.
Questions, as noted above, about what junior lawyers lose in terms of learning and tacit expertise when only reviewing the collated outputs of ML compared to primary engagement with legal documents.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the need for cautious, non-autonomous legal AI use and materially extends the cluster by explaining that ML systems shape lawyers’ attention while concealing their reasoning. It also shows why controlled proprietary data may mitigate security and hallucination risks without resolving opacity, though it does not directly establish that verification consumes efficiency gains.
qs: ML algorithms are interactive in that they define through their outputs what the lawyers come to focus on in decision-making, and hence what they are also blind to.
But few firms have such resources, and the black-box risk remains as the way algorithms make determinations using the data is still opaque.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI selectively reallocates bounded legal tasks while lawyers retain collaborative, contextual and accountable roles. It materially extends the synthesis through “mediated evolution”: a concrete explanation of how professional autonomy, partnership governance, data readiness, opacity and organisational context create uneven adoption and a persistent gap between technical capability and deployed use.
qs: Whilst then, there is evidence of algorithms replacing human tasks, when ML is used, the algorithms only replace certain tasks and hence collaboration with lawyers is needed to deliver advice to clients.
Hence, mediated evolution means there is a disconnect between what ML could theoretically do and how it is being used in actually existing ML applications in law firms.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that legal AI remains fallible and requires caution despite mitigation efforts. It cites hallucination-related sanctions and argues that proprietary-data models may address some risks but do not eliminate opaque decision-making; it does not, however, directly assess verification costs or establish empirical error rates.
qs: Lawyers are, then, rightly cautious about using ML.
But few firms have such resources, and the black-box risk remains as the way algorithms make determinations using the data is still opaque.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: Faulconbridge directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-driven legal change is shaped by organisational context and professional power rather than technical capability alone. His mediated-evolution framework emphasises path-dependent, non-linear change, while his account of professional autonomy and partnership governance explains why adoption is selective, slow and potentially resisted.
qs: Through the analysis the paper develops the concept of mediated evolution which is a way of conceptualising change in legal work that is material and meaningful, but which is also path dependent and non-linear and thus needs to be understood through situated analysis of the enactment in practice of change.

The role of autonomy in professional work results in decision-making about means and ends sitting with professionals, and hence they direct how change occurs, and can equally prevent change when it is considered a threat to their interests.

kp.k: Legal AI change follows mediated, not inevitable, evolution
kp.d: Faulconbridge argues that ML produces meaningful changes through interactions between technological possibilities and the legal profession’s institutions, priorities and strategic responses. His framework rejects a predetermined trajectory toward lawyer replacement: adoption is path dependent, non-linear and best understood through situated examination of actual practice.
qs: Mediated evolution is a way of conceptualising change in legal work that is material and meaningful, but which is also path dependent and non-linear and thus needs to be understood through situated analysis of the enactment in practice of change.
Trajectories of change will be mediated by the legal profession itself as it responds to the opportunities and threats experienced.

kp.k: Evidence draws on English research from 2018–2024
kp.d: The analysis combines primary and secondary sources. Primary research involved over 70 interviews across projects with lawyers, law-firm technologists and technology providers, supplemented in some cases by observations. Interviewed lawyers worked in firms ranging from the largest global firms to small/medium-sized UK firms, predominantly doing corporate work, with some consumer services. The research investigates actual adoption and non-adoption rather than supplying a profession-wide employment forecast; underlying data cannot be openly released for ethical and commercial reasons.
qs: Primary data comes from research in the English context between 2018 and 2024 examining the adoption of ML by law firms.

As part of a number of projects over 70 interviews have been conducted with lawyers, other members of law firms such as technologists responsible for implementing AI systems, and technology providers.
The firms predominantly focused on corporate work, although some also provided consumer services such as matrimonial and litigation advice.

kp.k: Extractive ML targets document-intensive corporate legal tasks
kp.d: The paper identifies established extractive ML applications in discovery, due diligence and initial review, including assessing whether contentious matters are viable. These applications identify and extract information for subsequent decisions or predictions, with corporate work particularly suited because of large document volumes. For most firms, off-the-shelf services rather than bespoke algorithm development drive change.
qs: In an extractive form, the main application of ML is to automate the process of identifying relevant aspects of a document/extracting information needed for decision-making.
this is most commonly part of discovery, due diligence or initial review stages (including for contentious work whether to accept a matter as a viable case).
for the majority of lawyers and law firms it is “off the shelf” applications, such as those in Tables 1 and 2, that are driving evolutions in legal work.

kp.k: Generative ML expands applications, but adoption remains cautious
kp.d: Generative ML adds content production to extraction and extends applications into smaller-scale corporate matters and some consumer work. The paper reports Womack’s 2023 survey finding that 50% of the top 50 UK law firms were not considering generative AI, while describing broader experimentation by 2024 through generic cloud-based models and software services. It does not provide an updated 2024 adoption percentage.
qs: In a 2023 survey of the top 50 law firms in the UK, 50% were not considering the use of generative AI (Womack, 2023).
By 2024 things have undoubtedly moved-on.
a key development with generative ML has been the expansion of the range of use cases, including into smaller scale corporate work and into some aspects of consumer legal work.

kp.k: Tasks, rather than whole lawyer jobs, are changing
kp.d: Using Abbott’s distinction between diagnosis, inference and treatment, the author finds that observed ML use primarily changes diagnosis: collecting and analysing information that supports defining problems and advising clients. This task-level account challenges predictions of occupational disappearance. The paper distinguishes theoretical generative capabilities from observed practice, reporting that most lawyers are not using generative ML for inference and treatment.
qs: When ML is used it predominantly has impacts at the level of specific tasks, rather than the job as a whole.

However, to date, most lawyers are not using generative ML to engage in inference and treatment work and software as service providers have focussed on tools that enable lawyers to more quickly assemble in report form the information needed to engage in inference work
Hence, mediated evolution means there is a disconnect between what ML could theoretically do and how it is being used in actually existing ML applications in law firms.

kp.d: Observed automation replaces substantial parts of document review, information collation and report preparation, while lawyers interpret outputs and provide advice. The research finds less time spent compiling information or producing boilerplate structures and more time investigating implications and tailoring documents to clients. Replacement of particular tasks therefore coexists with continuing lawyer involvement.
qs: Whilst then, there is evidence of algorithms replacing human tasks, when ML is used, the algorithms only replace certain tasks and hence collaboration with lawyers is needed to deliver advice to clients.

Spending less time collating and summarising key facts and information but more time reviewing summarised information and identifying further lines of enquiry to inform decision-making and “treatment”.
Being able to spend more time refining, and making bespoke for clients, key documentation with less time spent producing boilerplate contractual/legal structures.

kp.k: Junior training faces both disruption and possible redesign
kp.d: The author presents reduced demand for trainees and junior lawyers as a potential consequence, not a measured employment outcome. Automating diagnosis threatens document-based learning and tacit expertise, creating concerns that can slow adoption. Conversely, juniors may spend more time interpreting ML outputs and learning through collaboration with technology; firms are still working through how to reproduce training benefits.
qs: ML has the potential to reduce the number of trainee and/or junior lawyers needed, this feeding debates about reductions in the size of the legal profession (Law Society, 2021).
Many diagnosis tasks, such as document review, are seen as a crucial way of allowing trainees to develop their skills and experience.
Junior lawyers can often move from spending many hours collating data to spending much more time interpreting the implications of the diagnosis outputs of ML.

kp.k: ML supports preventive advice and broader service boundaries
kp.d: Rapid analysis of larger datasets can enable work previously too slow or costly, expanding lawyers’ roles from resolving bounded matters to anticipating risks and opportunities. In an observed example, employment-dispute documents from a large retail organisation supported branch-level risk profiles and preventive advice. The author argues these services move law firms toward advisory territory associated with management consultants, potentially changing service domains and clients.
qs: Second, when using ML lawyers can transform their role from problem solver to problem anticipator and preventer.
The patterns identified allowed a risk profile to be developed for each branch and in turn lawyers provided the client advice about anticipatory action to reduce the risk of future disputes.

They result in the reimagining of the boundaries that define the protected work of lawyers as new advisory services, more closely aligned to what other occupations such as management consultants might provide.

kp.k: Data readiness and confidentiality constrain implementation
kp.d: Although firms possess extensive documentation, the research finds that usable, curated datasets often require substantial investment. Lawyers raised unresolved questions about client consent, cross-client use of insights and possible leakage through models shared across firms. The author describes generative ML as heightening confidentiality concerns and notes that few firms can match the largest firms’ proprietary-data model initiatives.
qs: Whilst many lawyers have no shortage of documents – in paper or digital form – that could be the basis of a dataset, few have documents organised in a way that are useable by ML algorithms.
Significant investment is, therefore, needed to produce data warehouses.
Have clients consented to their data being used for ML?
What are the implications of advising one client using insights from ML that are based on the data of another client?

kp.k: Opacity and statistical reasoning reshape professional risk
kp.d: ML outputs influence what lawyers notice and overlook, while the reasoning behind extraction or generation may remain opaque. The paper links this to ethical concerns, liability anxieties and hallucinations, citing the 2023 New York fake-citation sanctions incident rather than a measured error rate. More fundamentally, it argues that turning documents into patterns, probabilities and visual outputs changes the basis of legal analysis; proprietary datasets do not eliminate black-box risks.
qs: ML algorithms are interactive in that they define through their outputs what the lawyers come to focus on in decision-making, and hence what they are also blind to.
The most highly publicised case in law involved two lawyers being fined after submitting fake citations, generated by ChatGPT, in a legal case in New York (Milmo, 2023).
The analyses that ML conducts transform documents into statistical patterns and probabilities.
But few firms have such resources, and the black-box risk remains as the way algorithms make determinations using the data is still opaque.

kp.k: Professional autonomy mediates slow, compartmentalised adoption
kp.d: The research finds resistance tied to professional identity, trust, learning, liability and client relationships. Partnership governance and lawyer autonomy mean implementation is negotiated rather than simply imposed. Adoption was often confined to individual teams or practice groups and concentrated on automation for cost savings; more advanced augmentation remained limited to a smaller set of first movers. The author treats professional responses as mechanisms shaping change, not proof that no change occurs.
qs: The most advanced augmentation-led changes are currently only found in a smaller number of first-mover firms
the adoption of AI technologies has been shown to be often limited in scale and scope (Rodgers et al., 2023).

As a result, our research, like that of Rodgers et al. (2023), found slow and often compartmentalised adoption restricted to one team or practice group and mainly the automation aspects of ML being used, as part of cost-saving efforts, with some of the more advanced augmentation possibilities yet to emerge.

kp.k: Technologists become active participants in legal service production
kp.d: ML requires multidisciplinary collaboration beyond traditional IT support. Observed technologist activities include prompt design, workflow creation, dataset selection, supervision of firm-specific learning and explaining ML to clients. These activities influence legal outputs and challenge lawyers’ autonomy and jurisdiction. The paper notes the UK’s alternative business structures permitting non-lawyer partners, but identifies unresolved challenges around technologists’ careers and professional boundaries.
qs: This goes beyond what an IT department has provided historically, because the individuals play an active role in legal work by configuring and supporting the use of ML.
Designing templates for and training lawyers how to prompt generative ML tools, with this prompt engineering influencing the kinds of outputs generated by the tool.
The pivotal role of technologists in the use of ML in law firms can challenge both the autonomy and protected jurisdiction of lawyers (Armour and Dicker, 2019).
Law firms have been multi-disciplinary spaces for a number of years, in the UK this being facilitated by alternative business structures that allow non-lawyer partners.

kp.k: Relational expertise underpins continuing human professional roles
kp.d: Drawing on Pakarinen and Huising, the author argues that lawyers contribute contextual understanding beyond documented datasets, persuasion and adaptive client communication, and trust grounded in professional accountability. These mechanisms support the expected persistence of human lawyers despite technical progress. This is a theoretical and forward-looking argument: the paper anticipates continuing value in professional regulation and distinguishes regulating lawyers’ AI use from regulating AI systems themselves.
qs: Such expertise is opaque to ML’s pattern recognition (as it is not documented in datasets) and thus difficult if not impossible to replicate.

Understanding how to convince different clients of the merits of a course of action, addressing their misgivings and adapting when prescriptions are not followed in intended ways is a crucial part of ensuring successful outcomes.

Lawyers are trusted because of the accountability system that differentiates them from, for example, consultants, this system existing because of the recognised risks for clients when dealing with legal matters (Abbott, 2005).
Debates continue about how to regulate AI, but for the foreseeable future the value of the professions and their regulatory infrastructure seem likely to remain high.

kp.k: Research should track actual evolving tasks and mediators
kp.d: The conclusion recommends longitudinal attention to what does and does not change, how lawyers respond, and how successive technological developments alter adoption constraints. Rather than centring job counts or occupational survival, the author prioritises changing tasks, roles and combinations of automation and augmentation. The proposed framework allows existing barriers to recede while new mediators emerge.
qs: Studies thus need to focus on actually existing uses of ML and not just the theoretical potential and hype that often surrounds discussions of change.

Change will not be teleological and hence careful analysis of what is and isn’t changing, the effects of the responses by lawyers, and the implications for the role of lawyers in society will be required.
The task, then, is to understand in an ongoing manner how as one set of mediators recedes others emerge and the implications for change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Faulconbridge argues that ML changes particular legal tasks rather than replacing lawyers' jobs wholesale.
pts.d: In the observed applications, extractive and generative ML primarily affect diagnosis: gathering, reviewing and summarising information that informs subsequent professional judgement and advice. Automation of this work combines with augmentation of lawyers, who interpret the outputs and formulate responses for clients. The author distinguishes this observed pattern from predictions of the profession's demise.

pts.k: ML reallocates lawyers' time from information assembly and boilerplate production towards interpretation and client-specific refinement.
pts.d: Faulconbridge reports qualitative findings that lawyers spend less time collating facts and producing standard documents, and more time reviewing summaries, investigating implications and customising documentation. He also predicts declining reliance on manual large-scale document review, summary-report production and template-based drafting, without specifying a completion date or quantifying time savings.

pts.k: ML may reduce demand for trainees and junior lawyers while changing how they acquire expertise.
pts.d: The author presents headcount reduction as a potential consequence, not a measured employment outcome. Automating document review could remove established learning opportunities, necessitating alternative training. Conversely, interpreting ML outputs could give juniors earlier access to more substantive work and reduce unproductive sifting. Firms remain uncertain about whether this reproduces the tacit expertise acquired through direct document engagement.

pts.k: ML enables predictive and preventive advisory services that extend lawyers' work towards management-consultancy-like activities.
pts.d: Faulconbridge argues that rapid analysis of larger datasets makes previously uneconomic diagnosis feasible, allowing lawyers to anticipate risks and opportunities rather than only respond to discrete matters. His research includes a retail-employment-dispute example in which lawyers used patterns in documentation to develop branch-specific risk profiles and recommend preventive action. The author suggests this changes service boundaries and potentially the client base; he does not report measured reductions in disputes.

pts.k: Generative ML broadens the range of legal use cases, while off-the-shelf products drive change for most firms.
pts.d: The author describes extractive ML as established particularly in high-volume corporate discovery, due diligence and initial review. Generative ML expands applications into smaller corporate matters and some consumer work. Most firms rely on vendor products rather than developing algorithms and infrastructure themselves; a few resource-rich, often very large firms undertake bespoke development and more advanced experimentation.

pts.k: Data requirements, confidentiality concerns and opaque outputs impede adoption and change the basis of legal analysis.
pts.d: Faulconbridge reports that poorly organised documents require investment in usable datasets, while client consent, cross-client learning and possible data leakage raise unresolved concerns. ML's statistical outputs influence what lawyers attend to and potentially overlook. Generative fabrication and uncertain provenance add risks. Proprietary datasets may mitigate some risks for well-resourced firms, but the author says opacity remains. These are reported barriers and concerns, not measured error rates or demonstrated leakage incidents.

pts.k: Professional autonomy, identity and partnership governance mediate adoption, producing slow and uneven change rather than technologically determined replacement.
pts.d: The author's central claim is 'mediated evolution': meaningful change shaped jointly by ML capabilities and professional institutions, priorities and risk management. Lawyers can resist changes that threaten valued tasks, training, client relationships or jurisdiction. The reported result is frequently localised adoption focused on cost-saving automation, rather than advanced augmentation. Faulconbridge predicts more lawyers working with AI, but through contingent, non-linear trajectories rather than an inevitable progression to autonomous legal advice.

pts.k: ML gives technologists an active role in legal work and requires negotiation of professional boundaries and careers.
pts.d: The research identifies technologists shaping prompts, workflows, datasets and supervised learning, and explaining ML to clients. The author argues that this exceeds traditional IT support: it influences substantive outputs and challenges lawyers' autonomy and protected jurisdiction. Firms must negotiate collaboration and roles for these specialists, while suitable career and partnership arrangements remain unresolved.

pts.k: Relational expertise and professional accountability are expected to sustain important human-lawyer roles even as ML improves.
pts.d: Faulconbridge argues that contextual knowledge not captured in datasets, reassurance grounded in judgement, persuading and adapting to clients, and professional accountability limit substitution. This argument draws on relational-expertise scholarship and professional theory rather than a direct comparative test. He treats the persistence of these roles as a qualified near-term and foreseeable-future expectation, not proof that all legal tasks are permanently immune to automation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main evidence is qualitative research from 2018–2024, supported by published research, a reported adoption survey and illustrative cases.
pts.d: Faulconbridge draws on more than 70 interviews across several projects with lawyers, law-firm technologists and technology providers, supplemented in some cases by observations of tool use. Firms range from global to small and medium-sized practices and predominantly undertake corporate work. The retail-employment example supports the claim about anticipatory advice. A cited 2023 survey reports that 50% of the top 50 UK firms were not considering generative AI; this is secondary evidence, not the author's own survey. The reported New York fake-citation sanctions incident illustrates risk, not a measured hallucination rate. Professional and organisational scholarship supports the conceptual interpretation. The supplied text offers no quantified causal estimates of productivity or employment effects, and its referenced tables and figure are not reproduced. Underlying data are unavailable publicly for ethical and commercial reasons.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings describe adoption through 2024; forecasts are conditional and generally have no fixed dates.
pts.d: The 2025 paper grounds its observed claims in 2018–2024 research, distinguishing established extractive applications from emerging generative experiments. Advanced augmentation is restricted to a smaller set of first movers. Wider change depends on usable data, resources, risk management, professional acceptance, training adaptations and collaboration with technologists. Most observed generative use supports information assembly rather than independently delivering inference and treatment. The author expects continuing evolution but explicitly rejects a predetermined endpoint, and argues that technical improvement alone need not remove institutional constraints.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are UK corporate law firms, junior and senior lawyers, technologists and their clients, with emerging applications in consumer practice.
pts.d: Junior lawyers face changing diagnosis work, learning pathways and potentially reduced staffing demand; lawyers delivering advice shift towards interpretation, bespoke work and relational judgement. Partners influence adoption through governance and professional autonomy. Technologists gain roles that shape legal outputs and client communication, creating jurisdictional and career questions. Large firms can fund bespoke tools and proprietary datasets, while smaller and medium-sized firms primarily access vendor products. Corporate clients may receive faster, more comprehensive and preventive advice, alongside confidentiality and reliability concerns. Some consumer work is included, but the source does not establish population-level access-to-justice effects or economy-wide legal employment changes.
